profile.name: Byung shin chum
profile.tagline: A Korean folk dance historically used by peasants to satirize the nobility.
profile.insight: Once a tool for peasant satire against the ruling Yangban class, this dance is now a subject of intense modern debate regarding its depiction of disability.
profile.profile: Byung shin chum is a traditional Korean folk dance originating in Miryang, Gyeongsangnam-do. Historically performed by peasants, the dance utilizes mimicry of physical impairments to mock the Yangban nobility. While revived in the 20th century by Gong Ok-jin, it remains a source of contemporary controversy due to its portrayal of disabled individuals.
profile.profile_long: Byung shin chum, literally translated as the 'dance of the handicapped,' emerged as a potent form of social satire within the agrarian communities of Miryang, Gyeongsangnam-do. Historically, the dance served as a subversive tool for lower-class peasants to mock the ruling Yangban nobility. By adopting the physical characteristics associated with various impairments—including paraplegia, hunchbacks, deafness, blindness, and leprosy—performers created a visual caricature of the elite, suggesting that the moral or social decay of the nobility was reflected in physical infirmity. Beyond these social critiques, the dance also incorporated characters and archetypes drawn from the rich traditions of Pansori and broader Korean mythology. The performance was not merely a display of movement but a theatrical act of resistance against the rigid social hierarchies of the era. During the Japanese annexation of Korea (1910–1945), the colonial administration banned the practice, labeling it vulgar and suppressing its public performance. Despite this historical interruption, the dance was later revived and brought to a wider modern audience through the work of the South Korean actress and dancer Gong Ok-jin. In the contemporary era, the dance has transitioned from a historical curiosity to a subject of significant ethical debate. In 2001, a performance in Daehangno, Seoul, sparked widespread criticism from disability rights advocates. Organizations such as the Research Institute of the Differently Abled Person's Right in Korea (RIDRIK) argued that while artistic freedom is a fundamental value, the specific form of this dance—which relies on the mockery of marginalized and alienated groups—is inherently problematic. Critics maintain that the dance perpetuates historical customs that humiliate disabled people, leading to a complex tension between the preservation of traditional folk performance and the modern imperative for social inclusivity and human dignity. Today, the dance exists in a state of precarious survival, recognized as a part of the Korean folk tradition while simultaneously facing scrutiny for its discriminatory content.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in Miryang, Gyeongsangnam-do, as a peasant performance intended to satirize the Yangban nobility. It was suppressed by the Japanese administration during the annexation period (1910–1945) due to its perceived vulgarity. It was later revived in the 20th century, notably by actress Gong Ok-jin.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. The dance involves the mimicry of physical impairments, including paraplegia, hunchbacks, deafness, and blindness.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Historically used as a satirical tool by peasants to mock the nobility. In modern times, it is a subject of controversy regarding its depiction of disabled persons.
sections.notable_figures: Gong Ok-jin (also spelled Kong Ok-jin), a South Korean actress and dancer who brought the dance to public attention.
sections.lineage: Part of the broader tradition of Korean folk dance and influenced by Pansori and Korean mythology.
